title: Blanton's tuberculosis and a morning with Fletcher Henderson
summary: Callender says the physical demands of big band bass and late nights with Ben Webster led to illness, and recalls Blanton playing with Henderson for hours.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Because I know Ben loved him dearly, and he dug Ben, you know. I think one of the factors in his early demise was hanging out with Ben, you know. [LAUGHS]

Well, when you play the bass, it's very physical. All music is physical, but playing saxophone your fingers work and your body doesn't necessarily perspire. But when you play the bass with a big band, you maybe have to change shirts or undershirts a couple of times a night. So this is how Blanton first contracted TB, just improper care, you know. You know, he'd work in Chicago or somewhere like that, you're wringing wet, and you go hang out with somebody like Ben all night, and then you get wiped out. Blanton was very frail. I don't think he weighed over 135 pounds to start with.

Anyhow, he and I and Lee Young and Sweepea, or Billy Strayhorn, used to hang out a lot together. And I remember once Fletcher Henderson lived out here, too, over on Hoover Avenue on the East Side. I remember one morning Blanton and I went by, and he played with Fletcher for hours. I just sat and marvelled. There was no such thing as tape recorders then, and wire recorders were big, bulky things, so you couldn't take them around. So that's why I say some of the best music has never been recorded. Because it's
just completely free... Blanton was also a genius with the bow on the bass, too. He could do anything.
